<reason>Both sides argued well, but B controlled the decisive clash. B set a clean burden (defend a screen you concede doesn't drive performance), landed a real contradiction in A's opening between "nobody can know which jobs don't need a degree" and "competition punishes useless screens," and neutralized A's framing objection ("if employers decide, the motion is vacuous") with the crisp antibiotics analogy — the motion names a habit and asks the decider to change it. Crucially, B gave a concrete, direct answer to A's strongest pressure question ("name the replacement filter for 4,000 résumés") with the broadened floor: degree OR relevant work OR apprenticeship OR military OR short screen, which cuts the pile just as fast, adds routes without closing the degree route, and therefore dissolves A's central "vacuum/goes underground" image. B also turned A's disparate-impact point on job-relatedness and closed with clear cost-asymmetry weighing. A's best material — fixed reading capacity, the transparency of a posted, earnable rule, and "the only gate with a published price" — was original and memorable, and A honestly resisted the claim that it had stipulated degrees predict nothing. But A's case visibly retreated from "the degree predicts performance" to "the degree is a convenient way to shrink a pile," which B named accurately and weaponized; and A never adequately explained why a rule-based broadened floor would be filled by referrals and gut rather than by the added rules. A also absorbed a small extra execution cost from a third clipped speech.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's answer to A's Q2: instead of dodging, B named a specific replacement first-cut (degree or work or apprenticeship or military or short screen) and showed it adds routes without removing the degree route — which directly dismantled A's "screening goes underground / vacuum" story, reinforced in the closing by "adding doors doesn't shrink the building."</best_rebuttal>
